_comment: Numbers the page renders. Upload a new copy of this file and the page
updates — no HTML change, no redeploy of anything else.
`decode` is a best recorded rate on that machine, or null for 'not
`prefill` is the same, for prompt processing, and is filled only where a
prefill rate was measured on that machine through that row's engine. Most
rows have none, which is why it is null far more often than `decode`.
measured'. Null renders as 'not measured' rather than a blank or a zero,
because a missing measurement and a slow one are different claims.
`modes` is how the model runs there: gpu = fully resident, ssd = experts
stream from disk, hyb = split CPU/GPU. Several modes means the app can
use any of them; an empty list renders 'does not fit'.
`os` and `backend` drive the two tab rows. os is mac|linux; backend is
metal|cuda|rocm|cann. Choosing an OS disables the backends that cannot run
on it, and the machine, post and download lists all filter to the pair.
A backend with no machine yet (cann) still renders a tab, disabled, because
'no measurement yet' and 'not supported' are different claims.
`ctx` is the window the model's own weights declare -- context_length in a
GGUF, max_position_embeddings in an MLX config -- with `ctx_tokens` the exact
integer it sorts on, `ctx_base` the trained window a RoPE/YaRN stretch started
from, and `ctx_src` the file and key it was read from. It is a file property,
not a measurement: null means nobody here has read it off that model.
`pick` and `class` curate the table. Every machine shows ONE row per size
class (small <=8B, mid ~30B, large ~125B, frontier/1M), chosen here rather
than offered as a menu: the reader gets our tradeoff and one click to see the
other 33 measurements. A row with no `pick` is still published and still
measured; it is simply not the default answer for its class.
`coding` is up to two PUBLISHED coding-agent benchmark scores for the row's upstream model,
full precision, not the quantised file: [{benchmark, value, setting, source_url, source_date, reported_by,
source_class}], SWE-bench Verified first, then Terminal-Bench 2.1 (the order the pick rule uses), else
another named benchmark. reported_by is 'vendor' or names the third party; source_class is 'primary' (read
from the cited page), 'verified-from-session' (found in an earlier session record and re-read at its URL)
or 'unverified-session' (shown in italics with a dagger, never used by the pick rule). No `coding` field
renders 'no published score'. `probes` is this catalogue's own checks on that row's server, kept apart:
{tool_call, check_17x23, date}. Both are written by flashrsi/local-mind-catalog/coding_cells.py.
_provenance: The M4 mini and DGX Spark rows were measured directly on those machines in August 2026 and carry the method in their notes. On 12 August 2026 three M1 Ultra rows were re-measured the same way and now carry medians with spreads: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Laguna-S-2.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Where a re-measurement moved a number it is recorded here rather than silently overwritten: Laguna-S-2.1 30.8 -> 33.4 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash 27.5 -> 28.0 (both faster than published), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 73.7 -> 72.3. The M1 Ultra DeepSeek-V4-Flash size was corrected from 97.6 GB to 87 GB: the old figure matched no file on the machine and disagreed with the same model's own M2 Max and DGX Spark rows. A fourth attempt, M2 Max Qwen3-4B, was WITHDRAWN rather than published: two runs of the identical script disagreed by 1.7x, so that row is now null. TWO LIMITS THIS EXERCISE EXPOSED, which apply to every row on this page. First, decode is not a single rate: measured on M2 Max, the 1->129 token slope and the 129->513 slope differ by 15%, because attention costs more as the context grows -- so any figure here depends on the token count it was taken at, which is 129. Second, these machines are shared, and a busy machine can halve the number; spreads are quoted so a reader can see when that happened. The remaining M1 Ultra and M2 Max rows are still carried over verbatim from the first version of this page and have NOT been re-verified. Prices are approximate street or list prices in August 2026, recorded so a rate can be read against what the machine costs -- they move, and they are not quotes. Muse Glimmer 30B was ADDED to the M1 Ultra and M2 Max boxes after the 12 August exercise and does not share its method: both figures are llama.cpp's llama-bench tg128 (build b10360, r=3, 12 August 2026), an instrument reporting a mean over repetitions rather than the median-of-paired-estimates used elsewhere here, so the two rows are comparable with each other but not strictly with their neighbours, and the notes say so. Where two runs exist the LOWER is published: M2 Max decode 6.42 and 6.25 -> 6.3, prefill 82.65 and 76.75 -> 78. Two figures also exist for the M1 Ultra and both are kept rather than one being chosen silently: tg128 23.20 and tg64 ~28.9. tg128 is published because the rest of the column is quoted at 129 generated tokens; the tg64 figure is not wrong, it is a shorter generation, which this page already records as producing a higher rate. The tg64 run is documented as having a ds4 Q4_K kernel substitution active and the tg128 runs do not say, which is why these rows decline to name an engine's kernels the way their neighbours do. These are also the only two rows on this page measured on TWO machines by one instrument, and the 0.28x ratio between them against a 0.605 tier prediction is the reason no rate here is scaled from another machine's. In late August 2026 a fifth box was added: an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo), running the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file as the DGX Spark row through the ROCm reference engine, at 15.0 tok/s decode. It is published at the machine's default power governor rather than at its best observed setting, because the default is what a buyer gets; forcing the GPU to `high` is worth +0.8% on decode and +6.7% on prefill, and up to +26% when the CPU is also busy, but it costs a co-running CPU job about 40% and was still showing 104C peaks after 25 minutes of soak, so it is not a free setting and is not what the row reports. The machine's NPU is excluded from the figure for the plainer reason that it was measured and is worth +0.4%. The Ryzen row's price is what was actually paid for the machine (£3,099, Bosgame M5, August 2026) rather than a list price, which is why it is the only row in a currency other than dollars; it has not been converted, because a made-up exchange rate is not better provenance than none. On 29 August 2026 two rows were added to the M1 Ultra table, each measured on that machine: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 30.8 tok/s and GLM-5.3-Flash at 24.1 tok/s. The GLM-5.2 row (3.5 tok/s, SSD-streamed) was removed rather than re-measured, because the model is no longer offered; its number was not superseded by a new measurement of the same model and is not claimed to be wrong. An Atlas A2 row (8x 910B2, 512 GB) was added in late August 2026 with a NULL decode rate: the ds4-rs-ascend binary is built and verified to install on that hardware, but DeepSeek-V4-Flash has not been run on it, and 'packaged' is not 'measured'. Its price is left blank: A2 systems have no citable list figure, and every other price here names a source, so an estimate was dropped rather than published as though it were sourced. FULL METHOD for the M1 Ultra rows, moved out of the rendered note on 2026-08-29 because that note had grown to 3,074 characters against 520 for the shortest box: Three of these six rows were re-measured on this machine on 12 August 2026; the figure is the median of paired estimates, not a best-ever run. Decode is isolated as the difference between a 129-token and a 1-token completion so prefill is excluded, and repetitions alternate A/B/B/A so drift lands on both arms. Each model runs on the engine the app picks for it, and they are not the same engine: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on llama.cpp with the ds4 kernels — 72.3, ten estimates spanning 67.5–78.0; Laguna-S-2.1 on the ds4 reference engine — 33.4, eight estimates spanning 33.1–34.3; DeepSeek-V4-Flash on our own Rust/Metal engine — 28.0, eight estimates spanning 27.8–28.2. The machine was shared with other work throughout, which is why the Qwen3.6 spread is the wide one; the DeepSeek figure independently reproduces a 27.9–28.2 anchor measured by a different harness. The last two rows are out-of-core rates and are still carried over unverified: GLM-5.2 is not present on this machine at all, and Kimi-K3 is present but its streaming mode is the untested claim — one attempt at an out-of-core model of that class drove the machine into 42 GB of swap and was stopped. Muse Glimmer 30B is measured by a different instrument and is marked so rather than blended in: llama.cpp's own llama-bench, build b10360, on 12 August 2026 — tg128 23.20 ± 0.19 over three repetitions, with a pp512 prefill of 247.55 ± 0.87. That is a mean over repetitions, not the median of paired estimates the rows above use. It is quoted at 128 generated tokens because that is nearest the 129 the rest of the column uses; the same model on this machine was separately recorded at ~28.9 tok/s on tg64, and that gap between 64 and 128 tokens is the context effect described below, not a contradiction. llama.cpp is the only engine that can load this architecture — our own engine has no path for it — but which of the two Q4_K matvec paths that run used is not recorded, so unlike the rows above this one names no kernels. Two rows were added on 29 August 2026 and both were measured on this machine. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 30.8, the median of three llama-bench tg128 repetitions (30.78 ± 0.03), running on llama.cpp; its prefill is 560.7 tok/s at pp512. GLM-5.3-Flash — 24.1, on the ds4 reference engine, fully GPU-resident at 32K context; the same model measures 17.6 at a 9,600-token prompt, so the headline is a short-context figure like the others on this table and long sessions are slower. GLM-5.2 has been removed from this row. It never fit in memory on a 128 GB machine — 216.7 GB, streamed from SSD — and GLM-5.3-Flash now runs resident on the same hardware at roughly seven times the rate, so the older model is no longer offered. The Atlas A2 note was removed from the rendered page on 2026-08-29 as telling the reader nothing the table already showed (decode is null, which renders as 'not measured'; price is null, which renders as nothing). Its content, for the record: A Huawei Atlas A2 server: eight Ascend 910B2 cards, 64 GB HBM each, 512 GB in total, confirmed from npu-smi on the box (8 chips, 65536 MB per chip, all reporting healthy). DeepSeek-V4-Flash has not been measured here. The ds4-rs-ascend controller is built and published for this hardware and installs on it, but no decode rate has been taken, so none is quoted — the row says 'not measured' rather than borrowing a number from another machine. An 87 GB model fits resident many times over in 512 GB, which is why the residency column reads GPU; that is an arithmetic claim about capacity, not a measurement of speed. No price is shown. A2 systems sell through configuration-dependent channels with no list figure to cite, and every other price on this page names a source — a list price, or an amount actually paid. An unsourced estimate would be the odd one out, so the field is left empty until there is something to point at. FULL METHOD for the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and M2 Max rows, moved out of the rendered notes on 2026-08-29 for the same reason as the M1 Ultra's: the page carried more method than a reader of a comparison table needs. AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395: The same DeepSeek-V4-Flash file as the DGX Spark row, 86.7 GB on disk, on a Bosgame M5 mini-PC (AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 “Strix Halo”, Radeon 8060S, 128 GB LPDDR5X, 2 TB SSD) through the reference ROCm engine, so the model and the quantisation are comparable to the Mac rows even though the engine is not. Measured August 2026 at a 2048-token context; eight baseline repetitions spanned 0.03 tok/s (15.00–15.03) and the GPU clock was sampled throughout (1707 MHz mean). The weights sit in unified memory rather than streaming, which is why an 87 GB model reports a resident rate on a 128 GB box. The price is what was paid, not a list figure, and it is worth reading beside the DGX Spark row rather than instead of it: this machine is the cheaper of the two and the slower of the two on this model. Two things specific to it are worth stating rather than hiding. The rate depends on the GPU power governor: this figure is the out-of-the-box auto setting, and forcing high moves decode to 15.1 and prefill by 6.7% — a setting, not a property of the silicon. And its XDNA2 NPU, which no other box here has, was measured co-executing the output projection: it is worth +0.4%, so it is not used for this number. The 126 TOPS on the box is the platform total across NPU, GPU and CPU; the NPU's own share of it is 50. M2 Max: The same catalogue, scored for 64 GB. Qwen3-4B was measured twice here on 12 August 2026 and the two runs disagreed by 1.7× — 43.4 tok/s and then 74.9 tok/s from the identical script, model and engine. The first run was taken minutes after a 2.3 GB file landed on the machine, so the machine's state rather than the model dominated it. The row is therefore withdrawn rather than published at either figure: a number that does not mean what it says is worse than an admitted gap. It will return when it can be measured on a quiescent machine. The other three rows are still carried over from the first version of this page and have not been re-verified — this machine currently has 27 GB of disk free, so the 22 GB Qwen3.6 and the 48 GB Laguna-S cannot be stored without freeing space, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 87 GB is out-of-core here, which is what the 2.9 would cost. Muse Glimmer 30B was measured on both this machine and the M1 Ultra, by the same llama-bench instrument and in the same window — tg128 6.42 ± 0.08, and 6.25 ± 0.25 on a re-run, published at the lower 6.3; prefill 82.65 and 76.75 on the two runs, so ~78. The point of measuring it twice is what it says about every unmeasured row on this page: this machine delivers 0.28× the Ultra's rate, where scaling by GPU tier would have predicted 0.605 and advertised ~14 tok/s to a Mac that gives ~6.3. A control model measured on both boxes in the same window ran 3.0× slower here too, so this is the machine and not something peculiar to Muse Glimmer. This is also the smallest M2 Max — 30 of a possible 38 GPU cores — so a fuller Max should beat it. On 30 August 2026 the two dense Qwen3 rows were added to the M1 Ultra by the same 129-vs-1-token differencing used on the M4 mini, so the two machines' dense rows are directly comparable: Qwen3-4B 130.2 tok/s and Qwen3-8B 87.6 tok/s (medians of 5). Both ran on llama.cpp with the ds4 kernels, which is the engine the app picks for dense Qwen; the same models on our own Metal engine reach only 26.9 tok/s, which is why the engine is named per row rather than assumed. On 30 August 2026 the two M4 mini rows were re-measured and corrected UPWARDS: Qwen3-4B 19.6 -> 36.2 and Qwen3-8B 12.0 -> 21.6 tok/s. The published figures were ~1.8x low because they had been taken on a slower engine than the one the app now picks for dense Qwen; the corrected numbers come from the same 129-vs-1-token differencing as before, and are confirmed by a second instrument on the same box (llama-bench tg128: 37.9 and 21.6). Separately, the M2 Max Qwen3-4B row withdrawn earlier for a 1.7x disagreement between identical runs is now EXPLAINED rather than merely withdrawn: that laptop runs with Low Power Mode enabled, which costs it exactly 1.73x (69.7 vs 40.3 tok/s on the same model and binary). The row stays null until it can be measured with Low Power Mode off, because a battery setting is not a property of the chip. Also on 30 August 2026 the M2 Max column was re-measured with Low Power Mode OFF, and three rows moved UP: Muse Glimmer 30B 6.3 -> 8.5, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 51.6 -> 62.3, and Qwen3-4B filled in at 81.1 (the row withdrawn earlier for a 1.7x disagreement between identical runs — the disagreement was this setting). That laptop had Low Power Mode enabled for AC as well as battery, which costs about 2.1x on a small dispatch-bound model and about 1.4x on a bandwidth-bound one, and it does NOT recover on cooldown, which is what distinguishes it from thermal throttling. These three are llama-bench tg128 medians taken in a window verified quiet; the 129-vs-1 differencing used elsewhere agrees with llama-bench within 5% on the two machines where both could be run, but could not be re-run here because the laptop went back into interactive use. A second lesson is folded into these numbers: benchmarking several models back-to-back penalises whichever runs later — the 35B read 53 following two other models and 62 sampled on its own — so each figure here comes from a single-model series. The two M2 Max rows left carried-over on 30 August 2026 were then measured too, with Low Power Mode off. DeepSeek-V4-Flash went 2.9 -> 7.2 tok/s (median of 8 across two independent runs, 6.63-7.49); at 86.7 GB it cannot be resident on a 64 GB machine, so this is SSD-streaming with a 39.9 GB expert cache, and it is the one rate on this page that is disk-bound rather than memory-bound. Laguna-S-2.1 re-measured at 25.8 against its published 26.4, so that row was already right and is now verified rather than carried over; it was taken on the tile-rs engine, which an earlier campaign measured at parity (1.01x) with the reference engine the app uses for that model. No row on this machine is now unverified. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash joined in 1.0.6: 2.9 tok/s decode and 70 t/s prefill on the M1 Ultra with the file on the internal SSD, measured 13 September 2026 on a 2048-token prompt. Only ~152 GiB of the 366 GB file is weights; the engram tables are read a row at a time from the file, which is why it runs at all on a 128 GB Mac and why the drive matters: the same file decodes at 0.54 tok/s from an external USB SSD. It does not fit a 64 GB Mac. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MTP joined in 1.0.7 and is the first model on this page measured on two machines by the same instrument in the same window since Muse Glimmer. It is antirez's Q2 file, 147 GB on disk, on his reference engine, run with multi-token prediction as the app runs it. It is a DIFFERENT FILE AND A DIFFERENT ENGINE from the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next row above it, which is Unsloth's UD-Q2_K_XL on llama.cpp at 30.8; the older row is kept rather than overwritten because it was not re-measured, and the two are not a before-and-after. Only about 45 GiB of the 147 GB file has to be resident: the per-layer embedding table, 95.37 GiB of it, is read a row at a time and never held in memory, which is the same disk-versus-memory split as the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash row and the reason a 147 GB model reports a GPU-resident rate on a 128 GB Mac and fits a 64 GB one. M1 ULTRA 128 GB, 2026-09-19, greedy, reference engine main 8db1d1d: 43.7-43.9 tok/s on open prose with 71.7% of drafts accepted, and 47.0-51.2 on code with 96.7%; 36.1-38.0 with MTP off. The prose figure is published because it is the LOWER of the two, the same rule used elsewhere on this page. Prefill is 498-516 t/s across 2k-8k frontiers on 2048-token chunks, published at 510. M2 MAX 64 GB, 2026-09-21, same binary and the --prefill-chunk 1024 the model's own notes advise for 64 GB: 23.6-24.3 tok/s on prose at the same 71.7% acceptance, 27.9-28.0 on code, ds4-bench steady decode 22.6/20.8/20.6/20.0 at 2k/4k/6k/8k, prefill 259/234/229/227, and a resident plan of exactly 43.19 GiB at 8192 context — so IT FITS. A CLAIM OF 50-60 tok/s ON A 64 GB MAC IS WHAT PROMPTED THIS MEASUREMENT AND IT IS NOT REPRODUCED: the best figure on the real machine is 28 tok/s, on code, which is the easiest content for a draft head, and plain decode is 16-23. The M2 Max lands at roughly 60% of the Ultra's decode and 45% of its prefill, which tracks memory bandwidth, and draft acceptance matches the Ultra's exactly at 71.7% on prose, so the shortfall is the HARDWARE and not the speculation. One caveat specific to this laptop, in the same family as the Low Power Mode finding above: the plain arms fell about 28% between the first and last pass, 23.3 down to 16.8 on prose, while the MTP arms held steady — the signature of a laptop-class chip under sustained load — so a range is published rather than a single number, and where in a run a figure was taken matters. One earlier claim is CORRECTED rather than quietly dropped: a run on the Ultra with 64 GiB locked away via --simulate-used-memory had reported the same speed as the full machine, and was cited as evidence about 64 GB Macs. That simulation was right about RESIDENCY — 43.19 GiB on both, which the real machine confirmed to the decimal — and wrong about SPEED, because locking memory away leaves the Ultra's memory bandwidth intact. Only the fit half survived contact with a real 64 GB Mac. Finally, the engine that generates every kernel for this architecture in our own compiler is verified bit-identical to the reference engine and measures 4.8-8.4% ahead on decode, but the app routes this model to the REFERENCE engine, so no figure on this page is taken from it. 2026-10-04: the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 AMD rows were re-measured on the latest engines — DeepSeek-V4-Flash on antirez main + PR #992 (14.7, was 15.0) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on the pr4 build with the selected-split env var (12.1, was 8.66-9.44). The V4.1 gap is the engine improvement, not the machine. 2026-10-04: four models added to the Ryzen row from llama.cpp llama-bench tg128 r=3 (Qwen3-4B 67.0, Qwen3-8B 38.2, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 56.1, Muse Glimmer 30B 11.5); the same instrument as the M1 Ultra's llama.cpp rows. ADDED 11 October 2026: the M1 Ultra Ternary Bonsai 2 27B row, 31.3 tok/s — the median of three whole runs, not the best of them. Method stated in the box note. It is the first row measured with repeated WHOLE RUNS rather than repetitions inside one run, and the reason is worth recording for every other row on this page: on this machine the same binary measuring the same model at the same context gave 28.33 and 31.10 tok/s in consecutive runs, each internally flat to under 1%. Repetitions inside a run measure the run; only repeating the run measures the machine. The published figure is therefore from the quieter measurement point (a 129-token prompt, spreads 1.7%, 0.1% and 0.4%) with the wider 256-token range disclosed in the note rather than averaged away. This row also differs from its neighbours in one way a reader should know: it is measured on the current engine, not on the engine in the released build. 2026-10-25: the Atlas A2 row’s NULL decode rate was FILLED, and the note saying DeepSeek-V4-Flash “has not been measured here” is withdrawn — it had been measured twice, on two stacks, and this page had not caught up. Neither number comes from our own ds4-rs-ascend controller, which still has no end-to-end rate on this hardware; they come from the two stacks that do run the model there, and the row names the engine for each. (1) vLLM-Ascend, Ascend w8a8 conversion, TP8 across eight 910B2 cards, speculative decoding on (dspark, 7 draft tokens, eager): median 34.98 tok/s over 24 A/B/B/A trials, 86-token prompt, 128- and 512-token greedy completions with end-of-sequence ignored, two warm-ups discarded, measured 11 August 2026. Out=128 gave 34.13 and out=512 gave 35.60; the trials spanned 28.58–41.52, CV 8.64%. That session was the first with external witnesses — per-trial host load, per-chip AI Core maximum and HBM, sampled outside the timed window — and it SUPERSEDES an unwitnessed 37.09 from an earlier session, which was about 6% high; that session’s 15.83 steps/s is the outlier against 13.94 and 14.19 from two later ones. The decomposition is steps/s 14.19 at CV 0.72% × 2.46 tokens per step (acceptance 0.21), and the 14.19 is published in the note as a NON-SPECULATIVE FLOOR rather than as a rate, because a speculation-off serve could not be run on that box: no second server fits in HBM and the running one is root-in-container. A vendor figure of “50+” exists for this hardware and is NOT this configuration — it pairs four-bit w4a8 weights with reasoning and code corpora, and our own witnessed sweep on the same server reads 74.55 on code and 85.44 on list output against 34.71 on prose, with the step rate invariant at 13.94–14.86 across all six workloads. Decode there is set by how predictable the output is, not by the accelerator. (2) llama.cpp CANN backend, q4_0, four of the eight cards, measured 30 August 2026: pp512 3.88 ± 0.05 and tg128 0.36 ± 0.00 tok/s, r=3, fully offloaded, 166 GB resident across four cards, no CANN errors, box load 12.60. The route to that number is itself the finding: the CANN backend has ZERO MXFP4 kernels and its MUL_MAT/MUL_MAT_ID accept only F16/F32/BF16/Q4_0/Q8_0, so loading the 144.34 GiB MXFP4 file with full offload silently put 95.2% of the weight bytes on the host CPU and aborted anyway; the file was requantised to q4_0 (149.02 GiB) to obtain an NPU path. The abort — error 107000, a kernel not found by name, surfacing under unrelated operators including the rope ramp and an in-place copy — was NOT a missing operator package: the object exists, its digest matches its manifest, and the symbol is present. It is CANN 8.5.2’s aclnn executor cache holding a device-specific binary handle without keying on the device, so the first operator on any card after the first dies. Controlled repro, seconds long: one visible device passes, two abort, four abort; disabling the executor cache passes 5/5 backends on four devices, and that is what the measured run used. ITS PRICE was measured rather than estimated, on the operator that dominates MoE decode: q4_0 at n=1 goes 178.4 microseconds / 141.1 GFLOPS to 2298.0 / 11.0, i.e. 12.9×; q8_0 at n=1 10.9×; q8_0 at n=4 11.2×. So the 0.36 is gated 11–13× by a software defect rather than by the silicon, and the note says so. A METHOD WARNING is recorded against that work by its own author: the first control run, a rope operator test reporting 448/448 OK, was taken with a single visible device and therefore COULD NOT FIRE — it held fixed the one variable that was the entire bug. Two things were seen and are NOT claimed: an end-to-end q8_0 run needs all eight cards and four were held by another tenant, and a nondeterministic NaN appeared once in a q4_0 matmul at m=k=2880 and not in the next run. A host-CPU-only figure for the MXFP4 file on the same box, pp512 16.59 ± 0.89 and tg128 1.29 ± 0.40, is deliberately NOT published: it was taken on a contended box (load 96–115) and it measures the Kunpeng host, not the NPU. On 31 October 2026 Qwen3-4B on the M1 Ultra was re-measured as a decode/prefill PAIR from one build and moved 130.2 -> 121.4 tok/s, gaining 1690 t/s prefill; its engine label changed from 'llama.cpp + ds4 kernels' to 'llama.cpp (llama-bench)' because no llama-bench build here reproduced the old figure (stock 119.0, tile-rs 112.4). A number that moved because the engine changed is not a regression, and the label moved with it. Qwen3-4B's download size read '2 GB' on the Mac rows for a 2,497,280,256-byte file and is corrected to 2.5 GB; the column is decimal GB, so 2 GB understated it by a fifth. The Ryzen row's 2.3 GB is the GiB figure for that same byte count and is left alone pending a check on that machine, since it may serve a different file. An audit matching table rows to catalogue entries by MODEL NAME also flagged the two 10.7 GB M4 rows, and they are right: those are IQ2_XXS at 9.93 GiB and IQ2_M at 9.97 GiB, not the Q4 files the name matched. On 31 October 2026 a CONTEXT column was added, read from the weights rather than from any model card: context_length in the GGUF header, max_position_embeddings in an MLX/HF config, one copy of each model on this machine, recorded per row in ctx_src. 44 of the 45 rows have a value; Nanbeige4.3-33B has none because no copy of those weights is on a machine reachable from here, and the Ryzen box was down for this exercise. Four of the M1 Ultra files read are byte-for-byte the ones that row was measured on (Qwen3-4B 2.5 GB, Laguna-XS-2.1 20.7 GB, DeepSeek-V4-Flash 86.7 GB, GLM-5.3-Flash 96.5 GB); the rest are a copy of the same model at another quantisation, and THAT ASSUMPTION IS NOT SAFE IN GENERAL. Prefill is excluded: time-to-first-token was 0.116 s and the rate is taken between the first and last token. A warmup run at 95.53 was discarded. All five ran inside one server process, so the spread is within-process and understates run-to-run variation. The machine was not idle — two unrelated llama-server processes held about 25 GB resident and ~45 GB of GPU memory was allocated — but GPU utilisation sat near 10% throughout and the five runs show no downward drift. Prefill is filled only where a prefill rate was measured on THIS machine through the SAME engine as the decode beside it, which is why most rows read “not measured”. GLM-5.3-Flash 156.6 t/s is the reference engine at --ctx 32768 --temp 0, fully resident. DeepSeek-V4-Flash is quoted as ~300 t/s because the measurement is a range, 300–304, best-of-3 at a 3000-token context against the C reference's ~255; it is an older arm than the 28.0 tok/s decode beside it, so the two are not from one run. Bonsai 2's measured prefill is an MLX figure, while its decode here is tile-rs, so it is not shown either. Qwen3-4B was RE-MEASURED on 31 October 2026 and its decode moved down, 130.2 → 121.4 tok/s, because the pair now comes from one build whose provenance is a commit rather than a label. The published 130.2 carried the engine “llama.cpp + ds4 kernels”, and no llama-bench build on this machine reproduced it: stock gave 119.0 and a tile-rs build 112.4. (An earlier version of this note said the tile-rs build had ignored the full-offload flag and run 16 layers on the GPU. That was wrong: the two builds print different columns — one reports GPU layers, the other reports thread count — and 16 was its threads. Its offload state is simply not visible in that output, and its lower rate is what a separately recorded measurement of tile-rs generated mat-vec predicts.) So the row is now stock llama.cpp 71adbf2c5, fully offloaded, on the catalogued 2,497,280,256-byte file: prefill 1690 t/s at pp512 and decode 121.4 tok/s at tg128, each the median of THREE SEPARATE PROCESSES at r=3 (pp512 1679.4–1693.7, tg128 119.5–121.7). Three processes rather than more repetitions in one, because the spread between processes was 1.84% against about 0.4% inside them — a single run's error bar would have understated it fourfold. This is not a regression: it is a different engine, honestly labelled. Laguna-XS-2.1 is new on 31 October 2026 and is the second row measured as a decode/prefill PAIR from one build: prefill 1392 t/s at pp512 and decode 94.4 tok/s at tg128, each the median of three separate processes at r=3 (pp512 1391.2–1411.5, tg128 93.7–96.1), on the catalogued 20,700,620,160-byte Q4_K_L file, fully offloaded. That build prints its thread count rather than its GPU-layer count, so full offload was established by VARYING the flag instead of reading it: at zero offloaded layers the same model gives 225 t/s prefill and 44.2 tok/s decode, so the setting demonstrably bites. The weights were read from an external volume, which costs load time only — at 19 GB resident on a 128 GB machine the measured rates are not storage-bound. ⚠ The Ryzen row below lists the SAME file as 19.3 GB, which is its size in GiB; this column is decimal GB, so the two rows will disagree until that one is checked on its own machine. Strata 0.2.9 is a second engine on this machine for the same model, on a different file: its own IQ3_S pack, 54.8 GB mapped plus a 28.8 GB n-gram table and a 5.2 GB draft layer — 88.8 GB downloaded. 51.0 tok/s is the standard suite's short case (fresh process, three repetitions, thinking on, 512-token cap) with 530 t/s prefilling 4K and 16K; a fixed 200-token story measured a median 47.2 (46.6–47.6 across two fresh processes and one warmed one), and the suite's twelve correctness checks passed 12/12. It is not comparable with the 30.8 tok/s llama.cpp row above — different engine, different file and a different instrument (the server's own timings, not llama-bench), so the 1.53× says nothing about the two engines alone. The draft layer was within noise here (median 47.2 with MTP, 47.3 without), although the release's manual reports +27% on an M5 Max; this chip is not covered by that measurement. The weights declare 262,144 positions; 64K was configured and 16K measured, with one manual prompt at 32K reading 525 t/s. Pictures were not tested. The full write-up is Strata 0.2.9 on the M1 Ultra. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Coder is the newest row and is a different file and a different engine from the V4.1 row above it: the GSQ-RCO Coder export in IQ2_XXS, 182.7 GB across six shards — 72.1 GB of transformer weights and a 110.6 GB n-gram table — where the row above streams a 366 GB UD-IQ1_S export through the reference engine at 2.9 tok/s. 24.8 tok/s is the median of three warmed 128-token generations and 207 t/s the prompt rate at 1,005 tokens (183 t/s at 36k), on stock llama.cpp (7071ba3) on Metal at -ngl 99 --lazy-mode on -ub 512 -np 4 -kvu -c 262144, re-measured 2026-11-05 after the context was raised from 32k to 256k: prefill on this model is length-dependent, and a single prefill figure without its prompt length is not a measurement. That 194 is the default 512 ubatch, because the -ub 1024 this row ran with until 4 November was copied from the AMD host and is 5.7% slower here — measured interleaved twice over the same minutes at 194.1/183.6 over 1005 tokens, 179.2/174.5 at 3,005 and 167.7/167.6 at 6,405, so the two agree only once the prompt is long enough for attention to dominate. 256 is worse again (179.1/167.2/158.1) and 2048 worse than that (184.8/156.7/153.3), so 512 is a peak and not an endpoint of a monotone trend. -fa on leaves prefill unchanged and halves decode to 13.5 tok/s, so it is off and stays off. Both are the server's own timings with cache_prompt off and one warm-up pass discarded, because the first pass over the lazily-mapped table is roughly four times slower than every pass after it. The row reads fully resident because the transformer weights are, at 71.8 GB of RSS; the 110.6 GB table is memory-mapped and faulted a row at a time, which is what lets a 182.7 GB download report a resident rate on a 128 GB machine. Summing the file's own tensor table gives 476.7 billion parameters, not the 748–763 billion its card advertises — 271.8 billion routed experts, 197.3 billion in that table and 7.6 billion elsewhere — and that agrees with its own quantisation: the 72.1 GB that is not the table holds 279.4 billion parameters at 2.06 bits each, which is IQ2_XXS exactly. About 16.1 billion are read per decoded token, 8.5 billion of them routed experts. The quantiser's own size_label says 192x212B, which counts the expert stack and not this file. Sage-S2.1-Flash is catalogued and not measured, and the reason is worth stating precisely because it is not a speed problem. It is the same architecture as GLM-5.3-Flash: all 58 keys of its text_config are byte-identical, and after normalising the model.language_model. prefix its 38,423 text tensors match that model's by name and shape with zero differences — the only added weights are a ~0.3B vision tower and eighteen scientific projectors, neither of which is on the text decode path. So its decode cost per token is fixed by the same 45 layers, 288 experts at 8 active, 4,096 hidden and MLA dims as the GLM row above it, and nothing in its own structure predicts a different rate. What it does not have is a GGUF: the publisher ships bfloat16 safetensors only, 642.8 GB in 129 shards, and a Q2 conversion here would land near the 96.5 GB of the GLM-5.3-Flash Q2 already on this machine. Producing one means downloading the full 643 GB first, and parallel range requests measured 23 MB/s from Hugging Face on this box (12 MB/s at 8 connections, 24 MB/s at 16 and flat at 48, so it is a per-connection-to-host ceiling and not a pipe we can widen) — about eight hours before conversion begins. The row therefore shows no decode rather than a number modelled from a sibling, because the app has not loaded these weights and cannot. SenseNova-Loop-9B is the other new catalogue-only row, and its reason is different: the weights ARE on disk, and no published GGUF conversion can be opened by the installed engine. Two conversions load and fail for two different reasons — AtomicChat's declares qwen35 and then carries 523 tensors where that architecture defines 427, the 96 extras being the mhc_* hyper-connection weights its loop mechanism needs; annelo's declares sensenova_loop, which the installed runtime has no architecture entry for at all. So it shows no decode for the same reason as the Sage row: nothing here has loaded these weights. Maxwell-V1-Flash is the newest row and the slowest in this catalogue by an order of magnitude — 0.17 tok/s decode — and it was measured TWICE, because the first explanation for the number was wrong. No llama.cpp has its maxwell_moe architecture, so it runs through the publisher’s own reference implementation: the stuchapin W4A16 AutoRound build, 20.25 GiB, loaded by transformers 5.23 with auto-round 0.16.1 on the MLX backend, trust_remote_code, on MPS. The first run read 0.172 tok/s with another process holding 46.2 GB and about 0.1 GiB free, and this note said the rate was a paging floor a quiet box would replace. A quiet box was arranged — 39.8 GiB reclaimable, held across two polls — and it measured 0.165 tok/s over 32 tokens, 4% slower. Doubling the headroom moved the rate by nothing, so the constraint is the path, not memory. A token reads on the order of 6 GB of weights; at a modest 100 GB/s that is 60 ms against a measured 6,059 ms, about 100× more. Nothing in that says the architecture is slow, only that this way of running it is. The weights are still on a USB volume, which the catalogue’s own rule treats as disqualifying, so the entry keeps its unevaluated badge. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-4B is the other row measured since the last note, and it is the faster of the two: 104.2 tok/s decode at tg128 and 1,552–1,619 t/s prefill at pp512, stock llama.cpp build 10964 through llama-bench, on a 2.58 GiB Q4_K_M file. Decode comes from two runs that agree to 0.6% (104.47 and 103.90, each the median of five repetitions) and is quoted as one figure; prefill's two runs differ by 4% with the second carrying ±136 against the first's ±0.5, so it is quoted as a range rather than a point. Both figures are marked provisional for two conditions this site's catalogue page says move a result by more than the differences worth reporting: the weights were read from a USB volume, and the host had several GiB of swap in use with a virtual machine resident. Those matter least for decode, because the 2.58 GiB is resident after load and the transfer path affects load time rather than the per-token loop, and most for prefill, which is the figure whose runs disagree. It is a text-only, short-context measurement: 512 tokens warm, not 250,000, and the vision path was not tested. Inkling-2-Mini is catalogued and not measured, and nothing here can load it. It is Thinking Machines' 128x1.8B MoE: 24 blocks, 6 prelude then a 12-block core run three times then 6 tail, so it performs 48 layer visits and any layer count quoted for it is a visit count. Two containers are listed because the same weights ship both as a 17.63 GB IQ4_NL GGUF and as a 17.33 GB MLX 4-bit checkpoint, and they need different engines. Neither engine here has it: our pinned llama.cpp has no inkling2_loop architecture, and our MLX engine has no plugin for it. The server that does implement it is ddalcu/mlx-serve, and its support is not on main — main claims Inkling Small only, and Inkling 2 Mini arrived in PR #1261, which is closed and unmerged. So the row shows no rate rather than a modelled one, and it is not a claim that the model runs anywhere on this page. Qwen3.5-9B Defiant is the newest row, measured on 2026-11-20 as three separate llama-bench processes at r=3 on the catalogued 6,979,975,392-byte MTP-Q4_K_M file, read from internal NVMe and fully offloaded: pp512 877.3/888.1/888.9 t/s and tg128 41.83/46.09/42.48 tok/s, quoted as the medians 888 and 42.5. Where the weights live does not change that number, and the arithmetic says why. The file is on an external USB volume, whose cold sequential read measures 218 MB/s against the internal SSD's 6.2 GB/s on the same command, and an 8 GB file does not stay in the page cache, so a disk-bound run would be slower than the cold rate, not faster. At 3.4B active parameters and 2.06 bits per weight a token reads about 0.88 GB; at the measured 25.3 tok/s that is 22 GB/s of sustained reads, which is 100x what the external volume delivers cold and 2.6x what it delivers even fully cached. The two Qwen3 rows were re-measured on this machine in August 2026, decode isolated as the difference between a 129-token and a 1-token completion so that prefill is excluded. The larger Qwen3 variants are absent because they cannot be tested here rather than because they are slow: 14B needs a download this machine has no room for, and 32B is a 20 GB file on a 16 GB machine with 12.7 GB free — it cannot be stored, let alone run. Speed at one bit-width is not comparable to speed at another. It appears twice because its published MTP draft model is worth 22% and does not come free: at the draft's default acceptance threshold it reaches 50.9 tok/s while accepting guesses the model itself would have rejected, so about half the continuation differs from ordinary greedy decoding; raising the threshold until the output is byte-identical leaves 42.3 tok/s, i.e. 1.4%. Both rows are measured, four runs each; the 42.0 row is the one to compare with anything else on this page, because every other decode figure here is the model's own output. Gemma 4 is here for the same reason — it fits the GPU at this width — and it answers a question worth recording: the draft model its authors publish, which makes their own engine 1.7 times faster, is worth nothing through this one (37.8 against a 37.4 tok/s median) and changes the output as well. A published draft model is not a published speed-up; the surrounding engineering does not come with the file. Gemma’s figure is the median of four runs that read 37.4, 37.4, 37.5 and 37.6; this row first showed the 37.6, which was the fastest of them rather than the middle one, and the column now carries the same kind of number as every other row on this page.
